questions.prompt: Meridian Fusion Consulting's owner invests $50,000 of her own cash to start the business. The company then borrows $20,000 from a bank, which it immediately uses to buy a server. What are total assets after both events, and why?
options: $50,000 — a bank loan is a liability, not an asset, so borrowed cash never counts toward total assets
$90,000 — both the cash received from the loan and the server purchased with it count as two separate new assets
$70,000 — the loan proceeds became a new asset (the server) while an equal liability (the loan) was created, so assets grew by exactly the loan amount and equity stayed unchanged
$70,000 — but only because equity, not liabilities, increased by $20,000 when the loan was taken out
questions.explain: Borrowing $20,000 and immediately spending it on a server converts cash into equipment — one asset form into another — while creating a $20,000 liability (Notes Payable) for the obligation to repay it. Assets rise to $70,000 ($50,000 cash + $20,000 server), liabilities rise to $20,000, and equity stays at $50,000: Assets ($70,000) = Liabilities ($20,000) + Equity ($50,000), exactly as the accounting equation requires.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per the accounting equation, every transaction must affect the equation in at least ________ places, by equal amounts — the principle called double-entry accounting.
questions.explain: Buying a server with a loan increases an asset and a liability at once; paying an employee in cash decreases an asset and increases an expense (which reduces equity) at once. This 'always at least two places, by equal amounts' property is double-entry accounting, and it's the reason every journal entry has at least one debit and one credit of equal value.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it actually is, per Lesson 3's mapping onto an Oracle Fusion ledger.
right: The fiscal periods used for reporting within that ledger
The assumption that a business's books record only that business's own transactions
The currency a ledger's balances are kept in
The structure used to classify transactions into accounts
questions.explain: The economic entity assumption is the idea that a business's books only record its own transactions, never an owner's personal finances or a sister company's. In Oracle Fusion, a ledger is defined by exactly three things: a chart of accounts (the structure for classifying transactions), a currency (what the ledger's balances are kept in), and a calendar (the fiscal periods used for reporting) — the entity concept, implemented as software architecture.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what 'debit' means, per this course?
options: Debit always means an increase, regardless of what kind of account it's posted to
Debit simply means the left side of an account; whether it increases or decreases a balance depends entirely on the account's type
Debit means an account has gone negative or overdrawn
Debit only applies to asset and expense accounts; liabilities, equity, and revenue don't have a debit side at all
questions.explain: Debit and credit are nothing more than labels for the left side and right side of an account. Whether a debit increases or decreases a given account depends entirely on that account's type (asset, liability, equity, revenue, or expense) — there is no universal 'debit is good/bad' or 'debit is increase' rule.

questions.prompt: Per this course's normal-balance table, which statement correctly describes how Liabilities and Expenses behave?
options: Liabilities increase with a debit and decrease with a credit; Expenses increase with a credit and decrease with a debit.
Liabilities and Expenses are both debit-normal, since both appear on the same side of a balanced journal entry.
Liabilities increase with a credit and decrease with a debit; Expenses increase with a debit and decrease with a credit.
Liabilities increase with a credit and decrease with a debit; Expenses also increase with a credit, since all accounts that aren't assets share the same normal-balance direction.
Liabilities increase with a debit and decrease with a credit; Expenses increase with a debit and decrease with a credit.
Liabilities increase with a credit and decrease with a debit; Expenses increase with a debit and decrease with a credit, but only when the expense is actually paid in cash rather than accrued.
questions.explain: Liabilities sit on the right side of the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity), so they're credit-normal: a credit increases them, a debit decreases them. Expenses decrease Equity, so they behave the opposite of Equity — debit-normal: a debit increases them, a credit decreases them. This is exactly the DEAD pattern (Dividends, Expenses, Assets, Draws are debit-normal; everything else is credit-normal).
questions.distractorExplain: Option D gets Liabilities exactly right, but makes one specific wrong move on Expenses: it assumes that because Liabilities, Equity, and Revenue all share credit-normal behavior, Expenses must too. That's the trap lesson 5 warns against — Expenses behave the opposite of Equity, not the same as it, precisely because an expense decreases equity rather than increasing it. Grouping Expenses in with the credit-normal accounts is the one meaningful detail this option gets backwards.

questions.prompt: Cash (an asset) is posted with $14,500 of total debits and $2,800 of total credits over its first week, per the T-account method from this course. What is the ending balance, and on which side does it sit?
options: $11,700 credit balance
$17,300 debit balance
$2,800 debit balance
$11,700 debit balance — which makes sense, since Cash is a debit-normal account
questions.explain: Totaling each side of the T-account and subtracting the smaller from the larger gives $14,500 − $2,800 = $11,700. The balance sits on whichever side had the larger total — here, the debit side — which is exactly where a healthy Cash balance should sit, since Cash is debit-normal.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the four-step method for recording a transaction, per this course, in the correct order.
items: Identify which accounts the transaction actually involves
Classify each account as an asset, liability, equity, revenue, or expense
Determine whether each account increased or decreased
Apply the normal-balance rule to decide which account to debit and which to credit
questions.explain: The method always runs in this order: first identify which accounts changed, then classify each one by type, then determine the direction of change, and only then apply the normal-balance rule to decide debit versus credit. Identifying the right accounts in step one is the step that requires real judgment — the remaining three steps are nearly mechanical once the normal-balance table is memorized.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the common debit-and-credit mistakes covered in this course.
options: Debit always means 'increase,' regardless of the account's type
A journal entry with unequal total debits and credits is simply wrong — never 'close enough'
It's possible for an entry's debits and credits to balance perfectly while the wrong accounts were still used
A normal balance is an unbreakable rule that an account's balance can never violate
Oracle Fusion's built-in validation automatically catches all four classic debit/credit mistakes, including the wrong-account mistake
questions.explain: A balanced-but-wrong entry (option C) and the requirement that totals must match exactly (option B) are both real, named points from this lesson. Option A is the single most common misconception the lesson opens with — debit means left, not increase. Option D is also false: a normal balance is a typical expectation, not an absolute law. Option E overstates what Oracle Fusion can catch — it enforces balanced journals at a system level, but it cannot catch a human who balanced an entry correctly while still telling the wrong financial story.

questions.prompt: Why is Inventory classified as a current asset, even though it might sit physically in a warehouse for weeks or months?
options: Inventory is noncurrent, like equipment or buildings, because it is a physical, tangible item
Inventory only becomes a current asset at the moment it is actually sold
Current versus noncurrent depends on how quickly an asset is expected to convert to cash or be consumed, not on its physical form — Inventory is expected to sell within the year
Current assets are, by definition, only Cash and Accounts Receivable; everything else is automatically noncurrent
questions.explain: The current/noncurrent split is based purely on timing — how quickly something is expected to convert to cash or be used up — not on how an asset looks sitting on a shelf. Inventory is expected to sell within a year (or one operating cycle), which is exactly why it counts as current despite being a physical good.

questions.prompt: Match each account to the account type it actually belongs to.
right: A liability — amounts owed to suppliers for goods or services already received
Revenue — an increase in equity from core operating activities like consulting
An expense — a decrease in equity from the cost of operating
An asset — amounts customers owe the business
Equity — amounts shareholders paid in exchange for ownership shares
questions.explain: Accounts Receivable is an asset (amounts owed to the business). Accounts Payable is a liability (amounts owed to suppliers). Common Stock is equity (what shareholders paid in). Service Revenue is revenue (an increase in equity from core operations). Rent Expense is an expense (a decrease in equity from operating costs) — the same five account types from Chapter 3, applied to five specific accounts.

questions.prompt: Palisade Creative Group completes a $9,000 branding project for a client on March 28. The client actually pays on April 15. What is the correct accounting treatment?
options: $9,000 of revenue is recognized on April 15, when cash is actually received
$9,000 of revenue is recognized on March 28, when the work was substantially completed; the April 15 collection creates no new revenue, it just converts a receivable into cash
$4,500 of revenue is recognized in March and $4,500 in April, since payment was delayed
No revenue is recognized until the client's payment clears the bank
questions.explain: Revenue is recorded when it's earned — when the business has substantially done what it promised — not when cash arrives. The March 28 entry debits Accounts Receivable and credits Service Revenue for $9,000; the April 15 entry simply debits Cash and credits Accounts Receivable, with zero new revenue, since the earning already happened.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about expenses and the matching principle, per this course.
options: Expenses should be recorded in the same period as the revenue they helped generate, not necessarily the period they were paid for
An expense is always recorded in the exact same period the cash for it is paid
A business that prepays a full year of insurance upfront should expense 1/12 of the cost each month as the coverage is actually used, not the full amount upfront
Electricity used in March but billed and paid in April should be expensed in April, when the cash actually leaves the business
Cost of Goods Sold is an example of an expense matched to the same period as the sale that generated it
questions.explain: The matching principle (option A) is the core idea: expenses belong in the period they helped generate revenue, which is exactly why prepaid insurance is expensed gradually as it's used (option C) and Cost of Goods Sold is matched to the period of the related sale (option E). Option B contradicts the whole lesson — expense timing is about when it's incurred, not when cash moves. Option D gets the March electricity example backwards: the lesson records it as a March expense (when used), with the cash payment in April being a separate, later event.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Equity = Assets − ________.
questions.explain: Rearranging the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity) gives Equity = Assets − Liabilities — equity is simply whatever is left over for the owners after every liability is subtracted from every asset, not a pile of cash sitting somewhere.

questions.prompt: Millbrook Bread Co. buys an $8,000 commercial oven, paying $2,000 cash and financing the remaining $6,000 with a note payable. Which journal entry correctly records this compound transaction?
options: Debit Equipment $8,000; Credit Cash $8,000
Debit Cash $2,000; Debit Notes Payable $6,000; Credit Equipment $8,000
Debit Equipment $8,000; Credit Cash $2,000; Credit Notes Payable $6,000
Debit Equipment $2,000; Debit Notes Payable $6,000; Credit Cash $8,000
questions.explain: Equipment (an asset) increased by the full $8,000 purchase price, so it's debited for $8,000. That increase was funded two ways: $2,000 of Cash decreased (credited) and a $6,000 Notes Payable liability increased (credited). Total debits ($8,000) equal total credits ($2,000 + $6,000 = $8,000) even though the entry has three lines instead of two — exactly what a compound entry allows.

questions.prompt: Put these steps for diagnosing an out-of-balance trial balance, per this course's systematic approach, in the correct order.
items: Re-add both trial balance columns to rule out a simple addition mistake
Compare this period's trial balance to last period's, looking for a missing or unexpected account
Scan for one-sided journal entries with no apparent counterpart
Apply the divide-by-9 and divide-by-2 tricks to the dollar amount of the imbalance itself
Re-verify each journal entry's own internal balance, starting with the most recent and largest
questions.explain: The systematic approach starts with the fastest check (re-adding the columns), then compares against last period, then scans for obviously one-sided entries, then applies the two arithmetic tricks to the imbalance amount, and only as a last resort re-verifies every journal entry one at a time, starting with the most recent and largest — exactly the order this lesson recommends so you don't re-check every transaction from scratch.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per this course's troubleshooting tricks, a trial balance imbalance caused by a transposition error (two adjacent digits swapped) will always be evenly divisible by ________.
questions.explain: Swapping two adjacent digits always produces a difference that divides evenly by 9. An imbalance of $360, for example, divides evenly by 9 ($40), which makes a transposition error plausible; an imbalance like $127 doesn't divide evenly by 9, ruling that cause out.

questions.prompt: A bookkeeper accidentally debits 'Office Supplies' instead of 'Equipment' for a $5,000 purchase, but still correctly credits Cash $5,000. What happens to the trial balance?
options: It will be off by exactly $5,000, since the wrong account was debited
It still balances perfectly — both sides remain mathematically equal, and a trial balance has no way to detect that the wrong account was used
It will be off by $10,000, since the error effectively doubles
It cannot be determined without knowing every other account's balance
questions.explain: A trial balance only proves that total debits equal total credits — it says nothing about whether the correct accounts were used. Debiting Office Supplies instead of Equipment for $5,000, while still crediting Cash $5,000, keeps both sides equal; the trial balance balances perfectly even though the financial statements built from it would now be wrong.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it actually is, per Lesson 16.
right: A detailed, specialized ledger tracking one category of transactions, like AP or AR
The ability to trace a GL balance back down to its underlying subledger transactions
The master record of all account balances, built from summarized postings
The engine that applies accounting rules to turn subledger detail into GL journal entries
questions.explain: The general ledger holds summarized balances across all accounts. A subledger (like Payables or Receivables) tracks one category of transaction in full detail. Subledger Accounting is the rules engine in between, turning that detail into correctly formed GL journal entries. Drill-down is the ability to trace a summarized GL balance back down to the individual subledger transactions that made it up — the detail is never lost, just summarized.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a period that is locked against further postings, but could still potentially be reopened for a genuine correction, is in the ________ state — one of the three period statuses this course describes.
questions.explain: Open periods accept new postings freely. Closed periods are locked but can potentially be reopened if a real correction is needed. Permanently closed periods are locked for good, typically once there's no realistic chance they'll ever need to be touched again — for example, after an audit is finalized.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes accrual accounting from cash accounting, per this course?
options: Cash accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash moves; accrual accounting records them only when cash actually changes hands.
Accrual accounting is required only for very small businesses and certain tax filings, while cash accounting is what GAAP and IFRS require for most other businesses.
Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash moves; cash accounting records them only when cash actually changes hands.
Accrual accounting records expenses when incurred, but still records revenue only when cash is actually received — mixing the two methods depending on which side of the transaction you're looking at.
There is no real difference between the two methods; both describe the same timing rules using different names.
Cash accounting and accrual accounting differ only in which account types they apply to — cash accounting governs expense accounts, and accrual accounting governs revenue accounts.
questions.explain: Accrual accounting records revenue when it's earned and expenses when they're incurred, regardless of when cash actually moves — this is the method behind the matching principle, and it's what GAAP, IFRS, and Oracle Fusion are all built around. Cash accounting, by contrast, waits for cash to actually move before recording anything, which can badly distort which period a business's performance actually shows up in.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D gets the expense side right — incurred, not paid, exactly like accrual accounting says — but keeps the revenue side on a cash basis, recording it only when cash is received. That's a real, half-correct mix-up: accrual accounting applies the same 'earned/incurred, regardless of when cash moves' rule to both revenue and expenses symmetrically. Applying it to only one side is exactly the kind of partial understanding this question is checking for.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the five-step revenue recognition model (ASC 606 / IFRS 15) covered in this course.
options: A single contract isn't necessarily all revenue at once — a product and a year of support can be separate performance obligations, recognized on different schedules
Revenue should be recognized when cash is received, regardless of when control of the good or service actually transfers to the customer
The transaction price must be allocated across each separate performance obligation, based on their relative standalone value
Identifying the separate performance obligations within a contract is one of the five steps
Under the five-step model, all revenue in a bundled contract must be recognized on the date the contract is signed
questions.explain: A bundled contract (like a license plus a year of support) is split into separate performance obligations, each with its own standalone value, and the total price is allocated across them (options A, C, D) before revenue is recognized as each obligation is satisfied. Option B describes cash-basis thinking, not the actual core principle — recognition is tied to when control transfers, not when cash arrives. Option E is also wrong: recognizing everything at signing is exactly the 'all revenue, all at once' mistake the five-step model exists to prevent.

questions.prompt: Match each adjusting-entry category to its definition, per Lesson 22's 2x2 map.
right: Paid in cash, not yet incurred
Collected in cash, not yet earned
Earned, not yet billed or collected
questions.explain: Accrued Revenue is earned but not yet billed or collected (interest a bank has earned but not yet received). Deferred Revenue is collected in cash but not yet earned (a prepaid annual subscription). Accrued Expense is incurred but not yet paid (wages earned by employees before payday). Deferred (Prepaid) Expense is paid in cash but not yet incurred (a year of insurance paid upfront, expensed gradually) — the single 2x2 map covering nearly every timing mismatch between cash and the income statement.

questions.prompt: Cobalt Courier Services buys a delivery truck for $40,000, expects to use it for 8 years, and estimates a $4,000 salvage value. Using straight-line depreciation, what is the truck's book value after 5 years?
questions.explain: Depreciable base = $40,000 − $4,000 = $36,000. Annual depreciation = $36,000 / 8 = $4,500. After 5 years, Accumulated Depreciation = $4,500 x 5 = $22,500. Book value = Cost − Accumulated Depreciation = $40,000 − $22,500 = $17,500.

questions.prompt: A US exporter sells €8,000 of goods to a German customer when the exchange rate is $1.12 per euro. The customer pays a month later, when the rate has moved to $1.15 per euro. What is the result, and is it a gain or a loss?
options: A $240 foreign currency loss
A $160 foreign currency gain
A $240 foreign currency gain, because the dollar value of the fixed euro receivable increased between the sale and collection dates
No gain or loss, since the euro amount itself never changed
questions.explain: At sale: €8,000 x $1.12 = $8,960 recorded as Accounts Receivable and Sales Revenue. At collection: €8,000 x $1.15 = $9,200 actually received in cash. The difference, $9,200 − $8,960 = $240, is a foreign currency gain, since the exchange rate moved in the exporter's favor between the two dates — the euro amount owed never changed, only its dollar value did.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the income statement from the balance sheet, per this course?
options: Both statements report the exact same information, just in a different column order
The income statement reports performance over a period of time; the balance sheet reports assets, liabilities, and equity as of a single specific date
The balance sheet covers a period of time, like 'for the year ended'; the income statement is a snapshot as of one date
The income statement only reports cash transactions, while the balance sheet reports accrual-basis transactions
questions.explain: The income statement is a video, covering a stretch of time ('for the year ended'), reporting revenue, expenses, and net income or loss over that stretch. The balance sheet is a photograph, dated 'as of' one specific instant, reporting what the business owns and owes at that moment.

questions.prompt: A corporation starts the year with $340,000 in Retained Earnings, earns $92,000 of net income during the year, and pays $30,000 in dividends. What is ending Retained Earnings?
questions.explain: The Retained Earnings roll-forward is: Beginning Retained Earnings + Net Income − Dividends Paid = Ending Retained Earnings. $340,000 + $92,000 − $30,000 = $402,000.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the cash flow statement, per this course.
options: A company can report strong net income while its cash is actually shrinking, because net income is an accrual-basis number that doesn't equal cash movement
Depreciation is added back in the operating activities section, because it reduced net income without ever actually using any cash
Proceeds from a new bank loan appear in the operating activities section
An increase in Accounts Receivable during the year is subtracted in the operating section, since it means less cash was actually collected than revenue earned
Purchasing new equipment appears in the financing activities section
questions.explain: Net income and cash flow are genuinely different numbers (option A), which is exactly why depreciation — a non-cash expense — gets added back in operating activities (option B), and a growing Accounts Receivable balance gets subtracted there too, since it represents revenue earned but not yet collected in cash (option D). Loan proceeds belong in financing activities, not operating (option C is wrong), and purchasing equipment belongs in investing activities, not financing (option E is wrong).

questions.prompt: Put these stages of the full accounting cycle, per this course's end-to-end walkthrough, in the correct order.
items: A journal entry is analyzed and recorded
The entry is posted to accounts and subledgers
Adjusting entries are made at period-end for accruals and deferrals
A trial balance is prepared and checked
Reversing entries are posted at the start of the new period
questions.explain: The cycle runs from a real-world transaction, through analyzing and recording a journal entry, posting it to accounts and subledgers, making period-end adjusting entries, preparing and checking a trial balance, building the financial statements from verified balances, closing the period, and finally posting reversing entries at the start of the next period before the whole cycle begins again.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: at year-end close (but not at a routine month-end close), revenue and expense accounts are closed out to zero, with their net effect rolled into ________, so the next fiscal year's income statement starts fresh.
questions.explain: Closing temporary accounts — zeroing out every revenue and expense account and rolling their net effect into Retained Earnings — is specifically a year-end step, on top of everything a routine month-end close already does.

questions.prompt: A balance sheet reports Total Assets of $403,000, Total Liabilities of $101,000, and Total Equity of $302,000. What does the fact that $403,000 = $101,000 + $302,000 actually confirm?
options: Nothing in particular; the equality is coincidental for this particular company
That the trial balance step was skipped entirely for this period
That every individual transaction during the period was recorded to the correct account
The accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity), formatted as a report — if this equality didn't hold, something upstream would definitely be wrong
questions.explain: A balance sheet is literally the accounting equation formatted as a report — Total Assets always equals Total Liabilities plus Equity by construction. If it ever failed to balance, that would be the single easiest sign that something upstream is definitively wrong. But, exactly like a trial balance, a balanced balance sheet doesn't prove every transaction used the correct account — it only proves the totals agree.
